slides.0.title: AOC rules and the Échelle des Crus
slides.0.subtitle: Reading Champagne through the INAO specification
slides.1.title: The skeleton of the AOC specification
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Legal basis and version
slides.1.highlights.0.content: The AOC was first recognised by the decree of 29 June 1936; the current product specification (cahier des charges) was approved by the order of 25 January 2024 and published on 28 January 2024
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Wine type
slides.1.highlights.1.content: The AOC is reserved for white or rosé sparkling wine made only by second fermentation in glass bottle; still wines belong to two other AOCs (Coteaux Champenois and Rosé des Riceys)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Permitted varieties
slides.1.highlights.2.content: The 2024 text lists seven principal varieties: Arbane, Chardonnay, Meunier, Petit Meslier, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris and Pinot Noir, plus the trial variety Voltis (Chardonnay Rosé was approved later; see Level 1)
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Proportion rules
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Vineyard: principal varieties ≥ 95% and Voltis ≤ 5%; in any one blend: principal varieties ≥ 90% and Voltis ≤ 10%, and Voltis alone is not allowed
slides.1.content: Every figure in this lesson follows the order INAO specification first, Comité Champagne second, third-party sources last.
slides.2.title: Hard rules for vineyard and harvest
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Density and pruning
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Row spacing ≤ 2.00 m, vine spacing 0.70–1.50 m, the two together ≤ 3.00 m; at most 18 yeux francs (true buds) per m²; pruning limited to Chablis, Cordon de Royat, Vallée de la Marne (Meunier only) and Guyot systems
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Prohibitions
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Irrigation is banned; pre-emergence herbicides are banned in the inter-row; headlands (tournières) must be permanently grassed and the inter-row must carry a cover crop from 30 November to 31 January
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Whole-bunch harvest
slides.2.highlights.2.content: The specification bans any harvest method that cannot pick whole bunches and requires whole-bunch transport and pressing, so machine harvest is effectively impossible; the start date is set under the rural code and the end date by prefectoral order
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Ripeness and alcohol
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Grapes must reach at least 143 g/L sugar in the must; base wines need at least 9% natural alcohol; after enrichment, total alcohol after prise de mousse may not exceed 13%
slides.2.content: The direction is consistent: whole bunches, gentle pressing and high acidity as the foundation for sparkling wine.
slides.3.title: Yield limits, reserve and pressing caps
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Two layers of yield
slides.3.highlights.0.content: The specification sets structural ceilings: a base yield of 12,400 kg/ha and a ceiling (rendement butoir) of 15,500 kg/ha; the marketable yield actually released each year is decided by the Comité Champagne in summer (9,000 in 2025 and 8,800 in 2026, shown only as yearly examples)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Reserve ceiling
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Where a reserve exists, each operator may hold base wine from at most 10,000 kg of grapes per hectare in production; extra yield to fill it needs an individual request, proof of quality control and stays under 15,500; reserve wine cannot carry a vintage
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Pressing cap
slides.3.highlights.2.content: At most 102 L of juice per 160 kg of grapes, so one pressing (1 marc) of 4,000 kg yields at most 2,550 L; the Comité describes this as 2,050 L cuvée plus 500 L taille; anything beyond counts as rebêche and must be distilled
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Minimum ageing
slides.3.highlights.3.content: NV: at least 15 months from tirage before release; Vintage: at least 36 months; disgorgement may not occur earlier than 12 months after tirage (details in ch-l2-6)
slides.3.content: Yield is a two-layer design: the specification sets the ceiling and the industry tunes supply each year with the marketable yield.
slides.4.title: Échelle des Crus: classification by village
slides.4.highlights.0.title: The unit is the village
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Champagne does not classify vineyards but villages (communes, called crus); the region has 319 crus (Comité Champagne key figures)
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Origin of the price scale
slides.4.highlights.1.content: A first scale appeared in 1911, growers and houses agreed it formally in 1919 and a 1952 decree fixed the bands: Grand Cru = 100%, Premier Cru = 90–99%, other villages 80–89%; the percentage was the share of the reference grape price a village received (sources differ on whether the 1911 scale was public)
slides.4.highlights.2.title: End of the scale
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Fixed grape pricing ended in 2004 under EU competition law (Taittinger, WineWithSeth), while the Comité Champagne FAQ says INAO dropped the scale in 2010. Both dates are shown and neither is tested; existing villages keep the Grand/Premier Cru terms under local, loyal and constant usage
slides.4.highlights.3.title: The current list and 42 vs 44
slides.4.highlights.3.content: INAO 2024: 17 villages may use Grand Cru (and Premier Cru), and 42 more may use only Premier Cru, all in the Marne département. Older material often says 44 Premier Cru (17/44/258 = 319); the gap of two is probably because the old scale listed Chouilly's black grapes and Tours-sur-Marne's white grapes separately as Premier Cru (our inference)
slides.4.content: The 42/44 gap and the 2004/2010 dates are source discrepancies: shown side by side here and kept out of the quiz.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
Under the INAO specification, what are the minimum months from tirage to release for NV and Vintage Champagne?
Specification: at least 15 months for NV and 36 months for Vintage, both counted from the tirage date.
How many villages may use the term Grand Cru in the INAO specification?
17 (Montagne de Reims 9, Vallée de la Marne 2, Côte des Blancs 6); 42 is the number of extra villages limited to Premier Cru and 319 is the total number of crus.
Under the rule of at most 102 L per 160 kg, how much juice may one 4,000 kg pressing (1 marc) give?
4,000 ÷ 160 × 102 = 2,550 L, which the Comité Champagne describes as 2,050 L cuvée plus 500 L taille.
